Fit a Bayesian multivariate state-space model

Source: R/mvgam_core.R
mvgam.Rd

Fits a state-space model in Stan. Each observation follows the observation family. On the link scale its mean is the sum of the effects in formula and a latent trend \(z_{t,s}\) for series \(s\) at time \(t\). The data never record the trend directly. trend_formula names how it moves from one time to the next, through a trend constructor such as AR(). It also takes predictors of the trend. With an AR(p = 1) trend: $$g(\mu_{t,s}) = \eta_{t,s} + \eta^{(z)}_{t,s} + z_{t,s}, \qquad z_{t,s} = \phi_s z_{t-1,s} + \epsilon_{t,s}$$ Here \(g\) is the link, \(\eta\) the predictor from formula, \(\eta^{(z)}\) the predictor from trend_formula and \(\epsilon\) the trend's innovation at each time. The overview article walks through a full analysis.

Usage

mvgam(
  formula,
  trend_formula = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  newdata = NULL,
  trend_map = NULL,
  loadings_prior = NULL,
  backend = getOption("brms.backend", "cmdstanr"),
  combine = TRUE,
  family = gaussian(),
  threads = NULL,
  save_pars = brms::save_pars(),
  run_model = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

Main observation model formula (supports brms syntax). Smooth specials s(), t2(), gp(), varying intercepts and slopes, monotonic mo(), measurement-error me(), distributional dpar sub-formulas and offset() are all available. gp() accepts both the approximate Hilbert-space form (gp(x, k = 20)) and the exact full-covariance form (gp(x), no k). Prediction at newdata requires the approximate form. An exact gp() term fits and scores in-sample. mvgam() says so once per session.

trend_formula

A one-sided formula for the latent process: a trend constructor such as AR() with any predictors of the latent state. Write lv_axis() in a term to vary its effect by latent factor, or by series in a model without factors, as in ~ x:lv_axis() + AR(). The series column itself is not supported in a term of this formula. Forecasting requires the approximate form of any gp() term here.

data

Data frame in long format, one row per series and time. A model with a trend needs a numeric time column and a factor series column, or the columns a trend constructor names through its time and series arguments. mvgam_data() checks a frame against a family before fitting. A list of multiply imputed data frames, or a mids object from mice, is also accepted. mvgam_multiple() describes the imputation path.

newdata

Optional held-out data.frame, stored on the fit as object$test_data. Fitting draws no forecasts. forecast() called without newdata forecasts these times, carrying the fitted latent state forward. plot(fit, type = "series") overlays them. posterior_predict() on these data uses the covariate part alone. The section 'Which prediction function?' of predict.mvgam() compares the two.

trend_map

Optional fixed factor loadings, in one of three forms:

  • a numeric n_series x n_lv matrix of loadings. NA entries are sampled. Finite entries stay fixed on Z in the posterior. An all-NA matrix fixes nothing and acts as trend_map = NULL

  • a data.frame(series, trend) assigning each series to one latent process

  • "identity", one process per series, or "shared", one process for every series

A factor model without a trend_map samples every loading. It identifies Z after sampling by a thin QR rotation (Heaps and Jermyn 2024). A trend_map with any fixed entry takes no rotation. The argument requires a trend_formula. The trend constructor takes a trend_map argument too. Supplying both is an error. loadings_prior lists the trend_map forms a structured loadings prior accepts.

loadings_prior

Optional named list giving a structured prior on the loadings of a factor model, such as species traits or a phylogeny. Most models leave it NULL. The section 'Structured loadings priors' of mvgam() describes its fields.

backend

"cmdstanr" or "rstan". Defaults to getOption("brms.backend", "cmdstanr").

combine

Logical. With imputed data, TRUE (default) pools the imputation fits into one and FALSE returns them as a list.

family

A description of the response distribution and link function, given as a family function, a call to one or its name. Supports most brms families, including the ordinal families (brms::cumulative(), brms::sratio(), brms::cratio(), brms::acat()). The brms families needing a separate linear predictor per response category, brms::categorical(), brms::multinomial() and brms::dirichlet(), are refused: use categ(), multi() and diri(), which take the categories in long format and share one latent structure across them. A family whose mean has to stay positive needs a link that keeps it there once a trend enters the linear predictor: pair stats::Gamma(), brms::weibull(), brms::exponential(), brms::frechet() and stats::inverse.gaussian() with link = "log". Their default links leave the mean positive only where the predictor is. A latent trend is centred near zero and reaches negative values, where the likelihood is undefined. mvgam() warns before fitting. brms::lognormal() is the exception: its mu is a log-scale location that takes any sign.

A family written inside a univariate brms::bf() is the model's family, as in brms. In a multivariate model each response may take its own family, in which case name it inside that response's brms::bf(): bf(count ~ x, family = poisson()) + bf(seen ~ x, family = bernoulli()). Passing a list of families to this argument, as brms::brm() allows, is not supported; the family belongs to the response that names it. A single family given here applies to every response that does not name one of its own. Closure-unit and multi-response families (occ(), nmix(), mvn(), mvt(), diri(), multi(), categ()) lay their data out by unit. Each models its response alone and cannot be one response of a multivariate model.

threads

Positive integer number of threads per chain, or NULL (the default) for none. The model is compiled with cpp_options$stan_threads = TRUE. cmdstanr then samples with threads_per_chain = threads. The closure-unit families (nmix(), occ()) and the multi-response families (diri(), mvn(), mvt(), multi(), categ()) split their likelihood over units with reduce_sum, in about eight chunks. With 50 or more closure units, threads = 4 samples about a third faster. Fewer units can sample slower, the threading overhead outweighing the gain. A brms family without a trend_formula uses the threading brms writes.

A brms family with a trend_formula samples each chain on one thread whatever threads says. The threaded likelihood brms writes leaves no place to add the trend. Each such fit warns.

save_pars

A brms::save_pars() object naming which parameters the posterior keeps. A model is built from working variables it also reports under another name: the standardised deviates a group-level block is scaled from, the unscaled coefficients a shrinkage prior scales, the ordered intercepts a mixture is identified by. Those are left out by default, as brms leaves them out. save_pars(all = TRUE) keeps every one. group and latent keep the per-level deviations and the latent values of a me() covariate. manual names individual parameters to keep.

run_model

Logical. FALSE builds the model without parsing, compiling or sampling it. The result holds $stancode, $standata and the prior table, with $fit set to NULL. stancode.mvgam_formula(), standata.mvgam_formula() and get_prior.mvgam_formula() return them. Methods that need draws, such as summary() and forecast(), refuse it. A jsdgam() model has no mvgam_formula(), which makes run_model = FALSE the way to inspect one before fitting. Defaults to TRUE.

...

Further arguments for the model and its sampler.

prior takes a brmsprior built with brms::prior(). Its rows replace the matching defaults. get_prior.mvgam_formula() lists every class a model takes, with trend classes carrying a _trend suffix. The plural priors is accepted as well.

chains, iter, warmup, thin, seed and control reach Stan as in brms::brm(). chains defaults to 4, each running 2000 iterations of which the first half are warmup. Results for publication should use at least four. The examples use two for speed. If the sampler reports divergent transitions, refit with control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95) or simplify the model. mvgam_diagnostics describes the checks. cores sets how many chains sample at once. It defaults to getOption("mc.cores") when that option is set and otherwise to one fewer than the machine's cores, up to chains.

silent sets how much the fit prints. 0 shows everything, Stan's own messages included. 1, the default, shows the sampler's progress and mvgam's notices. 2 prints warnings alone.

algorithm selects how the posterior is explored. It accepts "sampling" (the default), "meanfield", "fullrank" or "fixed_param" on either backend, plus "pathfinder" and "laplace" when backend = "cmdstanr".

init sets the starting values. It accepts "random" (the default), "0", a numeric value, a list or a function. With backend = "cmdstanr" it also accepts "pathfinder". That keyword runs Stan's Pathfinder approximation on the compiled model and draws one starting value per chain from it. Sampling then proceeds as usual from those values. It helps a model whose chains stall at a poor starting point or fill warmup with divergences. On a model that already warms up cleanly it adds about a second and lowers effective samples per second.

Five arguments shape the Stan program and reach brms unchanged:

  • knots gives knot positions by covariate name, for the observation and trend formulas alike.

  • drop_unused_levels decides whether a factor level with no observations still takes a coefficient.

  • sample_prior takes "no", "yes" or "only". Under "only" the observation likelihood drops out and the latent process keeps its prior. The draws then show what the model implies before any response is observed.

  • normalize = FALSE drops the normalising constants from the sampling statements. Sampling is faster and the posterior is unchanged.

  • save_model names a file to write the Stan program to.

Value

An object of class mvgam.

Structured loadings priors

A factor trend loads each series on a few latent factors through the matrix Z. By default each entry of Z takes an independent student_t(3, 0, 0.5) prior. loadings_prior replaces it with the structured prior of Heaps and Jermyn (2024). Each column of Z then follows a multivariate normal whose covariance Phi makes similar series load alike. Phi is the product of a kernel over series features and one factor exp(-d / theta) per distance matrix. The argument requires a trend_formula whose trend has latent factors.

The list takes these fields:

features

Per-series features, as a numeric matrix, a data frame or the name of an element of data2. Numeric, integer and logical columns are z-scored. An ordered factor is z-scored on its codes. An unordered factor or character column is one-hot encoded with every level kept (Heaps and Jermyn 2024, Section 6.2). Each encoded column takes its own length-scale.

distances

Pairwise distance matrices, as the names of elements of data2, a matrix or a named list of matrices. Each is rescaled to a largest entry of 1.

column_shrinkage

"iid", the default, shrinks no column. "mgp" shrinks later columns more strongly through the multiplicative gamma process of Bhattacharya and Dunson (2011), applied to the shared innovation scale. AR(), RW() and ZMVN() trends accept it. A VAR() trend builds its own innovation covariance. It takes "iid".

mgp_a1, mgp_a2

The hyperparameters of "mgp", by default 2 and 4. Heaps and Jermyn used an mgp_a2 of 3 and 6 in their two applications. A lower mgp_a2 shrinks less, for data that weakly identify the number of active factors.

Each length-scale takes a lognormal(0, 1) prior. Distances are rescaled to a largest entry of 1. A length-scale of 1 then gives a correlation of exp(-1) between the two most distant series. Heaps and Jermyn used the wider lognormal(0, sqrt(10)). A prior() on theta_features or theta_dist_<name> replaces the default. They rescaled a phylogeny to a root-to-tip distance of 1, which gives a largest pairwise distance of 2. Rescale a distance matrix before fitting to match their scale.

The prior applies to the sampled columns of Z. The reported loadings Z_tilde come from a QR rotation of them. Each column of Z_tilde mixes the sampled columns. shared_variation() and residual_cor() use Z Z', which the rotation leaves unchanged. The Identification section of trend_constructors describes the rotation.

A trend_map with no fixed entries, NULL or a matrix of NA, is compatible. jsdgam() passes the second form. A trend_map that fixes any loading is refused. Its free entries take the default prior of class Z, which the structured prior would duplicate.

Terms used in this documentation

Latent trend, latent state

The unobserved value \(z_{t,s}\) that the trend constructor evolves over time.

Innovation

The random change the trend takes at each time step, \(\epsilon_{t,s}\) above. Other texts call it a process error or a shock. cor = TRUE correlates the innovations of different series.

Fitted state, covariate part

The two versions of the trend a prediction can use. The section 'Which prediction function?' of predict.mvgam() defines them.

Prior

A distribution stating which values of a parameter are plausible before the data are seen. get_prior.mvgam_formula() lists the defaults.

Posterior draw

One joint sample of every parameter from the posterior distribution. Summaries and predictions average over the draws.

Hindcast, forecast

Predictions at the training times and after them. See hindcast.mvgam() and forecast.mvgam().

Closure unit

A site, or a site in one season, whose true occupancy or abundance holds across its repeat visits. See occ() and nmix().

ELPD, Pareto k

The expected log predictive density scores predictions of held-out data. Higher is better. A Pareto k above 0.7 marks an observation whose leave-one-out approximation is unreliable. See loo.mvgam().

Workflow

A typical analysis takes these steps:

  1. Check the data with mvgam_data().

  2. Choose a family (mvgam_families) and a trend (trend_constructors). Inspect the default priors with get_prior.mvgam_formula().

  3. Fit with mvgam(), then check convergence with summary.mvgam() and mvgam_diagnostics.

  4. Check the fit against the data with pp_check.mvgam() and plot(fit, type = "residuals").

  5. Interpret effects with conditional_effects.mvgam().

  6. Forecast with forecast.mvgam(). Compare models with lfo_cv.mvgam() or loo.mvgam().

  7. Report the model with how_to_cite() and methods_md().

See also

trend_constructors lists the latent trends. mvgam_families lists the observation families mvgam adds to those of brms. how_to_cite() writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model. methods_md() writes its equations. jsdgam() fits joint species distribution models. The overview vignette introduces the package. The data vignette sets out the data format. The forecast evaluation article scores and compares forecasts. The multivariate formula article fits several responses at once. The integrated distribution model article ties several observation families to one latent process.

Examples

# \dontrun{
# One count series with a smooth effect of a covariate x and an
# AR(1) latent trend, split into training and test times
set.seed(2)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(family = poisson(), n_timepoints = 100L,
                    trend_model = AR(), prop_trend = 0.5)
head(simdat$data_train)
#>    y   series time          x
#> 1  6 series_1    1 -1.2604710
#> 2  3 series_1    2  0.8094961
#> 3 19 series_1    3  0.2933053
#> 4  7 series_1    4 -1.3277923
#> 5  7 series_1    5  1.7753574
#> 6  4 series_1    6  1.7738998

# The parameters a model takes, with their default priors, before
# any fitting. A `prior` argument to mvgam() replaces any of them
get_prior(
  mvgam_formula(y ~ s(x, k = 5), trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1)),
  data   = simdat$data_train,
  family = poisson()
)
#>                   prior       class        coef group resp dpar nlpar lb ub tag
#>  student_t(3, 1.4, 2.5)   Intercept                                            
#>                  (flat)           b                                            
#>                  (flat)           b        sx_1                                
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5)         sds                                    0       
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5)         sds s(x, k = 5)                        0       
#>          exponential(2) sigma_trend                                    0       
#>          normal(0, 0.5)   ar1_trend                                   -1  1    
#>        source
#>       default
#>       default
#>  (vectorized)
#>       default
#>  (vectorized)
#>       default
#>       default

# A smooth of x in the observation model and an AR(1) latent trend.
# The test data are stored on the fit for forecasting
mod <- mvgam(
  y ~ s(x, k = 5),
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  data          = simdat$data_train,
  newdata       = simdat$data_test,
  family        = poisson(),
  chains        = 2,
  silent        = 2
)
#> Warning: 20 of 2000 (1.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
summary(mod)
#>  Family: poisson 
#>   Links: mu = log 
#> Formula: y ~ s(x, k = 5) 
#>    Data: simdat$data_train (Number of observations: 75) 
#>  Trends: AR(1) 
#>   Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; 
#>          total post-warmup draws = 2000
#> 
#> == Observation Model ==

#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sds(sx_1)     4.18      1.81     1.65     9.00 1.01      774      704
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept     1.55      0.15     1.25     1.85 1.00      855      843
#> sx_1          7.17      2.77     1.64    12.60 1.00      781     1120
#> 
#> == Trend Model ==
#> Trend Specific Parameters:
#>                       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS
#> sigma_trend[series_1]     0.54      0.08     0.38     0.71 1.00      837
#> ar1_trend[series_1]       0.46      0.17     0.11     0.76 1.00      522
#>                       Tail_ESS
#> sigma_trend[series_1]     1195

pp_check(mod)

# Forecasts of the test times, with the held-out counts overlaid
plot(forecast(mod))


# A methods paragraph with its references
how_to_cite(mod)

#> We used the R package mvgam (version 2.0.0; Clark & Wells, 2023) to
#>   construct, fit and interrogate the model. mvgam fits Bayesian
#>   state-space models that combine flexible predictor effects in both the
#>   process and observation components, using functionality from the brms
#>   (Burkner 2017) and mgcv (Wood 2017) packages. Observations followed the
#>   poisson family with a log link. The latent process followed AR(1)
#>   dynamics. The mvgam-constructed model and data were passed to Stan
#>   (Carpenter et al. 2017) via the cmdstanr interface (Gabry et al. 2024).
#>   We ran 2 Hamiltonian Monte Carlo chains for 1000 warmup iterations and
#>   1000 sampling iterations. Rank-normalised split Rhat and effective
#>   sample sizes (Vehtari et al. 2021) were used to monitor convergence.
